title: There are some names in Scripture people preach about with honor.
paragraphs: There are some names in Scripture people preach about with honor.
And then there are names people whisper.
The Book of Joshua does not hide Rahab’s past.
It puts it directly in front of you.

Not cleaned up.
Not softened.
Not edited for religious comfort.
“A prostitute named Rahab.”
That line alone has made generations uncomfortable.
Because religion has always struggled with the kind of grace God gives to people society already buried.
And maybe that is why her story still feels dangerous.

Because if God chose Rahab…
then nobody gets to say they are too ruined for redemption.
The city of Jericho was preparing for war.
Fear filled the streets like smoke.
Rumors spread everywhere about Israel’s God — the God who split seas, crushed Egypt, and marched through impossible wilderness with fire in the sky.
Jericho knew judgment was coming.

But while soldiers sharpened swords…
while kings fortified walls…
while proud men trusted defenses…
a rejected woman was listening.
And listening changed everything.
Joshua 2 introduces her with the Hebrew phrase:
“אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה” (ishah zonah)

A woman.
A prostitute.
The word “zonah” carries the idea of sexual immorality, harlotry, and social disgrace. In ancient culture, women like Rahab were not respected.

They were used.
Mocked.
Hidden in plain sight.
Men visited them in darkness and condemned them in daylight.
Rahab lived in the shadow section of society.
The kind of woman mothers warned daughters about.
The kind of woman religious men pretended not to see.
And yet…
when heaven looked at Jericho…
God saw her.
Not first for what she had done.
But for what she could become.
That is the part religion still struggles to understand.
God does not merely choose people based on their history.
He chooses people based on surrender.

While Jericho trusted walls…
Rahab trusted whispers about God.
Joshua 2:11 records one of the most shocking confessions in the Old Testament:
“For the LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.”
In Hebrew:
“יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים”
(YHWH Eloheichem Hu Elohim)
Rahab was surrounded by paganism, idolatry, and corruption…
yet somehow she recognized the true God before many Israelites ever fully did.
That should humble every church person reading this.
Because proximity to religion does not always produce faith.
Sometimes broken people see Jesus more clearly than proud people do.
Rahab hid the spies.
Risked her life.
Turned against her own city because she believed God was real.
This was not casual belief.
This was costly faith.
And faith always costs something.
The Hebrew language in Joshua suggests urgency and trembling throughout the encounter. Rahab was not operating from polished theology.
She was operating from desperation.
She knew judgment was coming.
And desperate people often recognize salvation faster than comfortable people.
That still happens today.
Some of the people closest to Jesus are not the polished religious experts.

They are addicts trying not to relapse.
Single mothers crying at midnight.
Men secretly battling pornography.
People smiling publicly while collapsing privately.
People who know exactly how broken they are.
Brokenness often becomes the doorway pride refuses to enter.
And then Scripture does something almost unbelievable.
God does not merely spare Rahab.
He honors her.
She becomes part of Israel.
Then part of the Messianic bloodline.
Then part of the genealogy of Jesus Christ Himself.
Think about that carefully.
When The Gospel of Matthew opens the genealogy of Christ…
Rahab’s name is there.

Not erased.
Not hidden.
Not excluded.
Included.
Forever.

The same society that would have rejected her…
God wrote into eternity.
That is grace.
Not modern motivational grace.
Biblical grace.
The Greek word for grace in the New Testament is:
“χάρις” (charis)

Unearned favor.
Divine kindness.
A gift impossible to deserve.
Rahab did not earn redemption.
Neither do we.
That is what makes the Gospel offensive to pride.
Because the cross destroys human ranking systems.
At Calvary, prostitutes and Pharisees stand equally in need of mercy.
Some people hate that truth.
Others are saved by it.
And maybe that is why Rahab’s story feels so personal.
Because deep down…
most people know what it feels like to be disqualified.
Maybe not by prostitution.
But by shame.

By divorce.
By addiction.
By abortion.
By betrayal.
By hidden sin.
By hypocrisy.
By failure.
By the version of yourself you hope nobody discovers.
Some people reading this still hear old voices saying:

“You’ll never change.”
“God could never use you.”
“You ruined your life.”
“You’re too dirty.”
“You waited too long.”
Rahab’s story crushes those lies.
Because God specializes in walking into condemned places and pulling out redeemed people.

Religion said:
“She is unclean.”

God said:
“She is Mine.”
And this is where the scarlet cord becomes unforgettable.
Rahab was told to hang a scarlet cord from her window so her household would be spared when judgment came.
Scarlet.
Red.
Blood-colored.
Not coincidence.
Biblical imagery constantly points forward toward redemption through blood.
The scarlet cord in Joshua whispers toward the cross long before Jesus was born.
Because salvation has always been about mercy covering judgment.
Always.
Even in the Old Testament.
Even in Jericho.
Even for Rahab.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to hear this clearly:
Your past may explain you.
But it does not own you.
Jesus Christ still transforms people everyone else gave up on.
The Greek word used repeatedly for salvation is:
“σῴζω” (sōzō)

To save.
To rescue.
To make whole.
Not partially rescue.
Whole.
That means God is not merely interested in managing behavior.
He restores identity.
Rahab was not remembered forever as “Rahab the prostitute.”
Eventually she became:
Rahab — ancestor of Christ.
That is what redemption does.
It rewrites names.
The enemy wants you chained to who you were.
Jesus calls you toward who you can become.
And the terrifying part about grace is this:

Some of the people most qualified to speak about Jesus…
are people religion almost threw away.
Because forgiven people love differently.

You can hear it in their worship.
See it in their tears.
Feel it in their gratitude.
People rescued from deep darkness rarely treat grace casually.
Rahab understood something many religious people still miss:

When judgment is approaching…
mercy becomes everything.
And this world is still trying to build Jericho walls.

Money.
Fame.
Sex.
Followers.
Politics.
Pride.
Self-worship.
But eventually every wall falls.
Only Christ remains.
That is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is rescue.
Rahab did not save herself.
She trusted the promise.
So do we.
And maybe that is why this story survives thousands of years later.
Because every human soul secretly wonders the same thing:
“Could God still want someone like me?”
Rahab answers that question forever.
Yes.
But surrender matters.
Faith matters.
Repentance matters.
Grace is free.
Following Jesus costs everything.
And still…
He is worth everything.
Be honest.
This hit harder than some expected.
And never forget this:
The same scarlet thread that hung from Rahab’s window still points broken people toward a bloodstained cross.
